title: The global gender-pay gap is narrowing too slowly because pay is embedded in care, occupational segregation, career progression, undervaluation, and bargaining institutions
source_unit: ILO new global gender-pay-gap estimates and Equal Pay International Coalition policy release, published 21 September 2026
geography: Global, with comparisons across country income groups and labour-market contexts

denominator.unit: ILO global gender-pay-gap estimate series released in September 2026

remaining_gap.value: women earn on average around 18% less than men globally

decade_change.value: the gap narrowed by only two percentage points since the previous estimates released in 2018

pace.value: the ILO describes the current decline as approximately 0.2 percentage points per year

observations.method: ILO global estimates summarized in an official news release; the release does not reproduce the complete statistical methodology or country-level series.
observations.uncertainty: An average global earnings gap is not a causal estimate and can conceal differences in hours, employment selection, occupation, sector, age, care, informal work, race, disability, migration status, and country definitions.
observations.subgroup: Women and men across countries and income groups, with additional exposure among caregivers, informal workers, low-paid workers, women in segregated occupations, and workers facing discrimination.
observations.counterinterpretation: A slow aggregate improvement can coexist with substantial progress in particular countries, sectors, cohorts, or legal reforms; the global average should not be read as a uniform experience.

denominator.unit: income-group comparisons reported by the ILO

high_income_change.value: the gap narrowed by around 2.5 percentage points in high-income countries over the past decade

lower_middle_change.value: the gap narrowed by around 2 percentage points in lower-middle-income countries

upper_middle_change.value: the gap narrowed by around 1 percentage point in upper-middle-income countries

policy_variation.value: some countries have made substantial progress, while others have seen gaps remain unchanged or widen

observations.method: ILO comparative estimates summarized by national income group; no country causal decomposition is provided in the release.
observations.uncertainty: Income-group averages can hide large within-group variation, different data quality, and changes in labour-force composition or measurement over time.
observations.subgroup: Workers in high-, lower-middle-, and upper-middle-income countries; women entering or leaving paid work; public- and private-sector workers; and workers in informal or precarious employment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Slower aggregate narrowing in some groups may reflect difficult-to-measure entry into paid work or structural occupational change rather than no improvement in women’s economic position.

observations.period: 2026; structural mechanisms behind the pay gap

denominator.unit: ILO diagnosis of structural drivers of gender pay inequality

employment_access.value: differences in access to employment contribute to gender pay inequality

career_progression.value: unequal career progression and occupational segregation contribute to the gap

care.value: the unequal distribution of paid and unpaid care responsibilities contributes to gender pay inequality

undervaluation.value: discrimination and the undervaluation of women’s work are identified as structural contributors

observations.method: ILO interpretive synthesis accompanying the global estimates; it does not quantify the contribution of each mechanism in the release.
observations.uncertainty: The mechanisms interact and may vary by country, occupation, family structure, sector, employer, and legal regime; the source does not establish a single dominant cause.
observations.subgroup: Caregivers, mothers, women in undervalued occupations, part-time and informal workers, women facing discrimination, and workers with limited bargaining or progression opportunities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed pay gaps can reflect multiple forms of sorting and preference as well as discrimination; mechanism-specific evidence is required before assigning one explanation or remedy.

observations.period: 2026; institutional routes proposed to accelerate equal pay

denominator.unit: ILO and EPIC policy-action set for equal pay for work of equal value

transparency.value: stronger pay transparency and objective, gender-neutral job evaluation are proposed measures

wage_policy.value: effective wage policies and enforcement of equality legislation are identified as routes to address structural inequality

bargaining.value: collective bargaining and social dialogue are presented as mechanisms to address undervaluation and give women a voice in shaping economic lives

care_protection.value: investment in care systems and social protection is included among measures that can address gender-pay inequality

observations.method: ILO policy statement and EPIC convening context; measures are recommendations and commitments, not evidence of adoption or effect.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not show which reforms are in force, who bears implementation costs, whether transparency changes bargaining power, or whether care investment narrows pay gaps without reducing job quality or access.
observations.subgroup: Women workers, employers, unions, governments, pay-setting institutions, care workers, families, and workers in occupations whose value is contested or undercounted.
observations.counterinterpretation: Transparency and formal equality rules can reveal gaps without correcting them; bargaining and care investment can be unevenly accessible and may leave informal, domestic, migrant, or subcontracted workers outside protection.

related_sources.claim: Equal Pay International Coalition context for cross-sector equal-pay collaboration.
ILO Equal Remuneration Convention No. 100 context for equal pay for work of equal value.

boundary: This record adds a gendered distribution and bargaining route: the global pay gap is changing slowly, while care, segregation, progression, undervaluation, transparency, collective bargaining, care systems, and social protection shape the conversion of formal equality into household economic power. It is an ILO estimate summary and policy statement, not a country-level causal decomposition, worker panel, employer audit, or proof that proposed measures close gaps.
